points.en: Step Nine has two tasks: to supply information and to give encouragement, both serving the action the counselee has chosen.
It comes late because information given before he is heard, clarified and has weighed options bounces off; once he has done that work he is ready to receive it.
Information is selected, not flooded: one or two scriptures that fit the action, opened with the counselee reading for himself, plus any practical facts he lacks.
Encouragement is specific: it names what he has already shown he can do in the sessions and ties it to the act ahead.
It anticipates the hard moment, such as his hesitating at his father's door, and gives a verse and an instruction to carry on anyway.
The key verse and next step are written on a card he takes home.
A sermon is broad and one-way; Step Nine is aimed at one counselee's chosen action and supplies only what he needs to carry it out.
The counselor opens the text and lets the counselee read for himself and say what it means in his situation, so the Word is information for his path rather than abstract doctrine.
A twenty-minute teaching floods the counselee, who cannot apply twenty things at once, so he is instructed but not helped.
The counselor should select only what this person needs for his chosen action, such as one or two scriptures and key practical facts, and withhold the rest.
Step Eight ends with the counselee choosing and confirming a specific action, preferably spoken aloud and written.
Step Nine equips that chosen action with the information and encouragement needed to carry it out, rather than supplying general teaching too early.
Supply only the information he needs for this action: one or two scriptures read with him and the practical knowledge he lacks, such as how to calculate and budget the tithe.
Encouragement is specific, naming the change shown in the sessions and anticipating the hard moment of the first gift when fear says he cannot afford it.
The counselor writes the plan or key verse on a card he can carry home.
He honestly admits the limit of his competence and does not pretend to know.
He refers the counselee to a trustworthy specialist (medical, legal, financial, or psychiatric) and offers to walk with him toward that help, which is a mark of maturity.
Written provision preserves what oral advice may lose and steadies the counselee in later weakness, doubt or forgetfulness.
The counselee takes away the chosen next step or action plan, relevant Scriptures and any referral contact details in writing.
The counselor's information and encouragement are only means the Spirit uses as He chooses, so Step Nine depends on the Holy Spirit.
The counselor is a fellow-paraklete, a junior helper alongside the Spirit, and prays before, during and after the session that the Spirit would prepare, supply and apply.
This guards against pastoral grandiosity: success is the Spirit's work, and apparent failure may still be completed by Him.
Generic encouragement ('You can do this') is weightless and cannot bear the real difficulty of the hour of temptation; it becomes background noise.

Real encouragement is specific: it names what the counselee has shown he can do, ties it to the coming act, and gives him a verse and instruction for the difficult moment, so it is a tool, not a wish.
